Published:
August 15, 2023
News
Provides a brief overview of the newest GovInfo API endpoint
Today, we are thrilled to announce the release of our highly anticipated
      Search Service as part of the GovInfo API. The Search Service enables
      searching of GovInfo content and metadata using the same search terms as
      on the website, allowing for complex queries to target specific documents.
      This opens up a new world of possibilities for developers using the
      GovInfo API.
Note:
This initial release should be considered a public preview for
feedback
, and there may be significant changes
      prior to the service reaching full production status.
Request
To issue a request to the service, issue a POST request to
https://api.govinfo.gov/search
with a request body that looks like:
{
        "query":"federal API",
        "pageSize":"2",
        "offsetMark":"*",
        "sorts":[
            {
                "field":"score",
                "sortOrder":"DESC"
            }
        ]
    }
Using our
interactive documentation
, simply copy the above into the request body field and click the execute
      button. If you need an API key,
sign up for one here
. To try the API before creating a key, use
DEMO_KEY
by
      clicking on the Authorize button at the top of the documentation page,
      adding it, and clicking Authorize.
This request is functionally equivalent to
this search
.
Request Parameters
Here is an explanation of the request parameters.
query:
Add search terms here; can include field operators like
collection
,
congress
,
lastModified
, and
        others, appropriate to collections. For more information on available
        search operators, see our
Search Operators page
and individual collection help pages.
pageSize:
The number of records to return per page. Maximum is 1000
offsetMark:
The starting record requested. For the first request, use
*
; subsequent requests should use the value from the
offsetMark
key in the response.
sorts:
Set the preferred sorting method, specifying fields and sortOrder. This
        can have multiple values, allowing for customized sorting. For the
        initial release, the recommended sorts are:
score -
equivalent to "Relevancy" in the user interface. This returns
          documents in the order where more relevant documents are returned
          first.
Note:
Sorting by score ascending is not supported.
publishdate, sortOrder:"DESC" -
equivalent to "Date New to Old" in the user interface. This returns
          documents with newer dateIssued values first.
publishdate, sortOrder:"ASC" -
equivalent to "Date Old to New" in the user interface. This returns
          documents with older dateIssued values first.
title, sortOrder:"ASC" -
equivalent to "Alphabetical (A-Z)" in the user interface. This returns
          documents with titles alphabetically.
title, sortOrder:"DESC" -
equivalent to "Alphabetical (Z-A)" in the user interface. This returns
          documents with titles reverse alphabetically.
lastModified, sortOrder:"DESC" -
returns documents based on the last added/modified time in GovInfo,
          with most recent documents returning first.
Note:
If not already specified, LastModified DESC is automatically set as a
          secondary sort to ensure that results are returned in a consistent
          order.
lastModified, sortOrder:"ASC" -
returns documents based on the last added/modified time in GovInfo,
          with most recent documents returning last.
The following parameters are optional:
resultLevel:
Determine whether the results should return results at the package-level
        ("package") or a mix of granules and packages ("default"). If not
        specified, the default will be used.
historical:
Determine whether to return documents that are not current (e.g. older
        editions of the CFR). If not specified as
true
, the default
false
will be used.
Tips
Here are some quick tips that may be of use with the Search Service.
if using quotes in your query, escape them with
\
use a range search with lastModified to limit your results to only
        results that have been added or updated since your last request. e.g.
lastModified:range(2023-08-15T12:00:05Z,)
Complex mods queries are available by using the
mods:
operator
        and including a mods field name, e.g.
mods:field:(@name:\"Geographic Scope\":\"Atlantic\")
Additional examples of Search Service requests are available on our
API repository on GitHub
.
Response
After a successful request, the Search Service will return a set of
      results formatted in json, with a set of fields intended to provide a good
      baseline of metadata and links for further exploration, including direct
      links to content and metadata.
For the sample request above, here is an example response.

Give us your Feedback
We are excited to hear your thoughts on the new Search Service!
To provide feedback, please create a new issue on the
GovInfo API GitHub repository
.
We will review user feedback and incorporate changes and enhancements to
      the Search Service in the future. Changes will be announced ahead of time
      via issues with an
upcoming label
and an
assigned milestone
.
Once we have a sense that the main
      functionality is satisfactory to the majority of users, we will remove the
      Public Preview label and announce the Search Service as production-ready,
      meaning that further changes will be enhancements only and non-breaking.

Democratic Republic of Congo Economic Update, October 2026: The Missing Link - When Firms Thrive, Jobs Follow
(
Washington, DC: World Bank
,
2026-10-28
)
World Bank
Show more
The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) entered 2026 with relatively strong macroeconomic buffers, but economic growth has been losing momentum and remains below the pace needed to achieve the country’s long-term development ambitions. Real GDP growth slowed from 9.3 percent in 2022 to 5.7 percent in 2025 and is projected to moderate further to 5.4 percent in 2026. Despite lower inflation, exchange-rate stability, and a narrower current-account deficit, growth remains heavily concentrated in mining, with limited benefits for the broader economy, employment, and poverty reduction. External shocks, including higher oil, fertilizer, freight, and insurance costs and the ongoing Ebola outbreak, are adding inflationary and fiscal pressures. Agriculture, small-scale commerce, and informal services, which employ a large share of the population, are particularly vulnerable to rising costs. Poverty remains widespread, while rapid population growth and sluggish job creation continue to constrain improvements in living standards. DRC’s mining-led growth model generates relatively few jobs, while informality, limited access to finance, infrastructure and logistics gaps, regulatory burdens, corruption, and weak managerial and workforce capabilities constrain the growth of productive firms. Micro and small enterprises account for a significant share of formal employment and job creation but face substantial barriers to investment and expansion. Strengthening access to finance, improving infrastructure and logistics, reducing regulatory and tax burdens, strengthening institutions, and building firms’ managerial and technological capabilities could improve productivity, encourage formalization, and create more productive jobs. In the near term, targeted measures are needed to protect vulnerable households and preserve macroeconomic stability, while medium-term reforms should promote private-sector development, economic diversification, and stronger links between growth, employment, and poverty reduction.

Western Balkans Regular Economic Report No. 30, Fall 2026: From Market Entry to Export Endurance
(
Washington, DC: World Bank
,
2026-10-23
)
World Bank
Show more
The growth performance of the six economies of the Western Balkans (WB6) has been better than expected in 2026, despite the multiple shocks affecting the region. This outturn reflects a degree of resilience in the region’s economic fundamentals, especially in comparison to advanced economy neighbors in the European Union (EU), which have suffered more directly from the impact of the conflict in the Middle East. Domestic demand has provided a critical anchor for the Western Balkans this year, but there remains a need to raise the rate of potential growth through structural reforms and higher productivity. Following a slowdown from 3.7 percent in 2024 to 2.6 percent in 2025, regional growth is estimated to have edged up to around 3.1 percent in 2026. Growth in the euro area, the region’s main trading and investment partner, weakened to 1 percent, implying that the WB6 grew about 2 percentage points faster than the EU during the year.

Population Thresholds and Classification Stability: Evidence from the World Bank’s Small States Classification Rule
(
Washington, DC: World Bank
,
2026-11-03
)
Han, Baran
Show more
The World Bank uses a population threshold of 1.5 million as the operational reference point for its Small States classification, with implications across several financing frameworks. This paper asks whether there is a break at the threshold in the macroeconomic outcomes associated with small country size, and how the classification rule should be administered given that population estimates are revised. In cross-country data for emerging market and developing economies over 2000–24, growth volatility, trade openness, and terms-of-trade volatility decline smoothly with population size across regression, nonparametric, and threshold-test evidence, with no detectable break at 1.5 million or at any alternative cutoff between 1 and 10 million. In a newly assembled real-time data set of 15 annual vintages, half of the published population estimates are revised by more than 1 percent within five years, and an estimate that is 1 percent above the threshold faces roughly a one-in-four probability of being revised below it within five years. Of the three Small State status changes since 2019, two resulted from revisions, not demographic change. Within the existing threshold-based framework, the paper evaluates four implementation rules, including the current single-year rule, and recommends an asymmetric persistence requirement—immediate entry and exit only after three consecutive years above the threshold—supplemented by an advance-notice flag based on estimated crossing probabilities.

Strengthening Road Safety Management: System Review Guidelines
(
Washington, DC: World Bank
,
2026-09-30
)
Global Road Safety Facility (GRSF)
Show more
Road safety practice is concerned with managing the safety of the road transport network by a system comprising multiple public institutions focused on improving safety performance. In good-practice countries, a designated lead agency plays a defining role in specifying, directing, and integrating this system management process. The guidelines presented here outline procedures that policy makers can use to review a country’s system management process, identify system management strengthening priorities, and specify initiatives to address them. They build on experience gained from the previous editions of Global Road Safety Facility (GRSF) guidelines which supported implementation of the recommendations of the World Report on Road Traffic Injury Prevention. Those recommendations addressed road safety at the system level and placed top priority on establishing a lead agency to guide the national road safety effort. The guidelines presented in this report reinforce this priority and the related recommendations. The guidelines are designed to support efforts by senior government officials and specialists in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) responsible for country road safety to strengthen system management processes and scale up road safety financing. Review findings enable the identification and prioritized specification of system management strengthening initiatives in LMICs that address shortfalls in road safety performance. The guidelines take a pragmatic approach to meeting this challenge. They recognize that under-resourced management processes at the system level are a major barrier to progress that must be overcome if sustainable performance gains are to be achieved. The guidelines refer to a country management review, as they are designed for applications mainly at the national government level. They can also address all levels of government - national, state, city, and local - separately or in some combination. The guidelines allow for flexibility in their application. Country differences must be identified during the review preparation phase to ensure that review procedures are adapted to them. Review findings will differ, depending on country contexts. Irrespective of the level of country capacity, the review procedures remain the same.

From Cities to Corridors: Unlocking the Philippines’ Urban Growth Potential
(
Washington, DC: World Bank
,
2026-10-26
)
World Bank
Show more
This report assesses how cities and urban corridors in the Philippines can function as catalysts for the country’s next growth push and job creation. The report applies the spatial lens of economic growth and convergence to the Philippines. As economies grow from low to high income, production concentrates in places like cities, coastal areas, or other better-connected locations, leading to unbalanced development with regional disparities. A successful spatial transformation hinges on economic integration policies that capitalize on the immediate benefits of concentrated production and translate them into convergence in living standards of people across space (World Bank 2009). This report focuses on the potential of urban areas in the Philippines not only as engines of growth but more importantly as centers of integrated regional development, contributing to spatial convergence in living standards across the country.
